questions.question: Why is embedding an entire 40-page contract as a single vector a bad idea?
options: It exceeds the embedding model's token limit
The averaged-out vector can't be close enough to any specific question to retrieve the right passage
Vector databases can't store vectors that large
It costs too much to compute
questions.explanation: One vector for a long document averages all its topics together. Retrieval can't pinpoint the specific clause that answers a question.

questions.question: A finance team indexes tax memos that have clear section headings (Nexus, Apportionment, Credits). Which chunking strategy fits best?
options: Fixed-size at 200 tokens with no overlap
Structure-aware chunking that splits along section boundaries
Semantic chunking that uses embeddings to find topic shifts
Embed the entire memo as one chunk
questions.explanation: When documents have clear structure, splitting along natural boundaries (headings, sections) produces coherent chunks that each cover one topic.

questions.question: Why add overlap between adjacent chunks?
options: To increase the total number of chunks for better search
To preserve context that crosses chunk boundaries — like references to 'the threshold described above'
To make the vector database index faster
questions.explanation: Overlap (typically 10-15%) ensures that sentences or ideas split at a chunk boundary still have enough surrounding context to be meaningful.

questions.question: What is the most common root cause of bad RAG retrieval that chunking can fix?
options: The model is not powerful enough
Chunks are cutting ideas in half or mixing multiple topics into one embedding
The vector database is too slow
questions.explanation: If chunks split a rule from its context or merge unrelated topics, the embedding can't represent any single idea clearly. Fixing chunking fixes retrieval.
